rules.statement: Hash, verify and judge a password in its Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC). Never use NFKC or NFKD, and never use the bytes exactly as submitted.
rules.why: The same visible text can be written as different code-point sequences, so hashing it as submitted gives one visible password two hashes. NIST SP 800-63B-4 §3.1.1.2 and RFC 8265 name NFC. NFKC and NFKD fold compatibility characters together, which merges passwords that look different.
rules.check: Look for password hashing, verification or policy code that never calls string.Normalize(NormalizationForm.FormC), or that uses FormKC or FormKD.

rules.statement: A password policy counts the length of a password in code points of its NFC form and checks blocklists with the NFC form. Its callers pass the password as submitted.
rules.why: The length has to be the length of what the store hashes. Otherwise a decomposed spelling passes as long enough, or gets past a blocklist that lists the composed spelling.
rules.check: Look for a length check that uses string.Length or UTF-16 units, or the un-normalized text, and for a blocklist lookup on the submitted form. Also look for callers that normalize before they call the policy.

rules.statement: Put password normalization inside the password hasher, not in each caller or each store. Stores and callers pass the password exactly as submitted.
rules.why: If the hasher owns the form, every store that uses it gets that form without its own code. A store that normalized for itself could not verify a stored hash of the submitted form, and every caller would repeat the same code.
rules.check: Look for Normalize calls on passwords in stores, endpoints or account services, rather than in the hasher.

rules.statement: When password verification compares the normalized form, verify the NFC form first. If that fails and the NFC form differs from the submitted form, verify the submitted form too, and report a match as SuccessRehashNeeded. Run this fallback for every hash, not only for hashes that some format marker identifies.
rules.why: Older stored hashes of the submitted form must keep verifying and then be replaced. Running the fallback whatever the hash format keeps verification time from revealing the account's hash format.
rules.check: Look for verification that returns Failed without trying the submitted form, that returns plain Success for a fallback match, or that only runs the fallback after checking a hash format or version marker.

rules.statement: Decode, normalize and re-encode password bytes only in sensitive (pinned, zeroing) buffer rentals, and dispose them as soon as the hash or verification is done.
rules.why: Intermediate copies of a password are secret material, and the secure pool pins them and zeroes them when they are returned.
rules.check: Look for password text or bytes held in ordinary strings, arrays or non-sensitive rentals while normalizing, and for rentals that are kept past the hash or verify call.

rules.statement: When a password cannot be normalized (bytes that are not valid UTF-8, or a string with an unpaired surrogate that string.Normalize refuses), hash or verify it as given instead of throwing.
rules.why: Such input spells no text that could be normalized, and it must still hash and verify the same way every time.
rules.check: Look for password normalization that lets an ArgumentException from string.Normalize or a decoder failure escape.

rules.statement: Server-side password paths in an ASP.NET Core Identity integration must not call UserManager methods that run IPasswordValidator: CreateAsync(user, password), ResetPasswordAsync, AddPasswordAsync and ChangePasswordAsync. Hash with UserManager.PasswordHasher and store the hash through IUserPasswordStore instead.
rules.why: The default validators enforce composition rules that NIST forbids, so they would refuse passwords that the server's own policy accepts.
rules.check: Look for calls to those UserManager password methods in integration code instead of PasswordHasher.HashPassword plus IUserPasswordStore.SetPasswordHashAsync.

rules.statement: Rotate the security stamp when a password is reset or changed. Keep the stamp when only rehashing the same credential, and treat a failed rehash update as non-fatal.
rules.why: A new credential must invalidate existing sessions. A rehash keeps the same credential, and the old hash still verifies if the update is refused.
rules.check: Look for a reset or set-password path that saves without UpdateSecurityStampAsync, a rehash path that rotates the stamp, or a rehash path that fails sign-in when UpdateAsync is refused.

rules.statement: A library that decorates a service the host may register (for example, a hasher that ASP.NET Core Identity registers with TryAdd) must handle both registration orders. Replace the last non-keyed registration in place, keep its lifetime, and wrap its instance, factory or implementation type. If none exists, add the decorated default. Never wrap a service that is already decorated.
rules.why: Hosts register the service before or after the library call, and TryAdd keeps an earlier registration. Wrapping twice would apply the decoration twice.
rules.check: Look for decorator registration that only uses Add or TryAdd, that changes the lifetime, that ignores ImplementationInstance or ImplementationFactory, or that has no guard against wrapping twice.

rules.statement: When a component requires a decorated dependency that can need request services, check for it when the component uses it, not at startup. If it is missing, throw an InvalidOperationException whose message names the fix.
rules.why: A dependency that needs request services cannot be built before a request exists, and the message tells the host how to fix its registration.
rules.check: Look for startup or IValidateOptions checks that resolve scoped services, and for type checks that fail with a generic message or not at all.
